questions.q: Show, don't tell: 'The market was very crowded and noisy.'
questions.a: Something like 'Shoulders brushed mine at every step; above the bargaining din a vendor's cry rose and fell.' A wrong answer adding intensifiers ('extremely crowded and very noisy') reveals the student thinks showing = stronger adjectives — it's actually swapping evaluation for evidence.

questions.q: Which ending earns marks: 'And that's why honesty is the best policy' or 'Grandmother's torn note lay in my palm — the five rupees I'd almost kept, now heavier than anything I'd ever held'?
questions.a: The second — the insight is dramatized through an image the story built; the first is a bolted-on proverb that could close any essay. A wrong answer reveals the student believes conclusions exist to state morals rather than to land meaning.

questions.q: Fix this tell: 'I was very nervous before the race.'
questions.a: Something like 'My spikes felt wrong on my feet; I retied them twice, then a third time.' A wrong answer 'I was extremely nervous' shows the student reaches for intensifiers — the tell-tale sign they haven't learned that nervousness lives in actions, not in the word.

questions.q: Narrative and descriptive essays follow the show-don't-tell contract: scene before summary, senses before ______, specific detail before general claims.
Fill in the blank: Narrative and descriptive essays follow the show-don't-tell contract: scene before summary, senses before ______, specific detail before general claims.

Fill in the blank: The transformation drill IS the lesson: 'The room was messy' → show it: 'Books lay spine-cracked on the bed; a week of biscuit packets fossilized on the desk.' Same fact, one ______ marks.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student converts tell-statements into show-sentences using sensory detail and specific verbs, and structures a narrative arc with an earned closing insight — no morals bolted on ('And thus I learned honesty is the best policy').
